analysis.one_liner: Strips federal oversight and capital rules from large nonbank financial companies like insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo a core piece of the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial reform: the system that lets the Federal Reserve directly supervise large nonbank financial companies — big insurers, finance companies, and asset managers — that are not banks but are big enough to wreck the economy if they fail. It would erase the Financial Stability Oversight Council's power to designate those firms, wipe out heightened capital and leverage requirements, end required reporting and resolution plans, lift a ban on management interlocks, and repeal the 2010 law that lets the Fed oversee payment, clearing, and settlement utilities. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never taken up again [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Large nonbank financial companies — big insurers and finance companies that post-2008 rules made subject to Federal Reserve supervision — would gain the most. They would be freed from enhanced capital and leverage requirements, Fed examinations, periodic reporting, exposure disclosure, and resolution-planning requirements, cutting their compliance costs and freeing capital. Payment, clearing, and settlement utilities would likewise be freed from Fed risk-management oversight.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates all Federal Reserve supervision of domestic and foreign nonbank financial companies, including heightened standards and minimum leverage capital requirements [S2].

Repeals the Financial Stability Oversight Council's authority to designate systemically important nonbanks and to require them to report credit exposure and file rapid-resolution plans for failure [S2][S3].
Repeals the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act of 2010, removing Federal Reserve risk-management oversight of financial market utilities [S2][S3].
Lifts the prohibition on management interlocks between supervised nonbank financial companies and other financial companies, and ends related reporting requirements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on the broader economy and ultimately taxpayers: the firms most likely to need a rescue in a crisis would be back outside enhanced supervision, with no minimum leverage capital requirements, no exposure reporting, and no resolution plans on file. Regulators would also lose the data and studies meant to help them wind down a failing giant without contagion.

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave large nonbank financial companies — the kind of firms whose distress spread the 2008 crisis — outside enhanced capital, leverage, and resolution-planning rules, increasing the chance that a failure again forces a public rescue [S2].

It repeals the requirement that regulators study how financial companies can be resolved through bankruptcy and coordinated internationally, and eliminates the Council's study of contingent capital requirements — tools aimed at making failures cheaper for the public [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill does not shrink any firm or end any bailout authority; it simply removes supervision of nonbank giants while leaving bank holding companies subject to those same standards, which is a rollback rather than a fix for too-big-to-fail [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings go to a small set of very large financial firms in the form of lower capital and compliance costs. The risk goes to everyone else: less buffer, less data, and fewer plans for winding down a failing giant, in a system that needed a public bailout the last time this oversight did not exist. The bill offered no replacement mechanism to contain the risk it would un-shackle.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, drew zero cosponsors, and expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S1][S4][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on January 23, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S1][S5].
No committee action, hearing, or floor vote ever followed; the action history ends at the referral [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its two-year life [S4].
When the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, the bill died with it, and the Dodd-Frank nonbank supervision framework it targeted remained in place [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The post-2008 oversight framework stayed intact, so the public kept the supervisory rules the bill would have repealed; the large nonbank financial firms that stood to be freed from Federal Reserve supervision gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public kept the oversight; big firms gained nothing

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee, where it received no further action.

against.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee leadership never scheduled the bill for consideration after its referral; the action history ends there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only visible supporter was its Republican sponsor: it drew zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a recorded vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (big insurers, finance companies, asset managers)
industries.note: The bill would free these firms from Federal Reserve supervision, heightened capital and leverage standards, examinations, exposure reporting, and resolution plans. Their gain — lower capital cushions and compliance costs — comes at the public's expense, since undercapitalized giant failures are what historically trigger taxpayer rescues [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Payment, clearing, and settlement utilities (clearinghouses and exchanges)
industries.note: Repealing the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act would end Federal Reserve risk-management oversight of these market utilities. Their cost savings come from operating with less oversight of a plumbing role whose failure can freeze ordinary payments [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (Federal Reserve, Financial Stability Oversight Council, Office of Financial Research)
industries.note: The bill would strip these regulators of their authority over nonbank giants and the data-gathering tools that support it. Their interest in keeping the tools runs alongside the public's interest in crisis prevention [S2].
